issues.legal_issue: The ordinary time limit for reassessment does not bar a transitional reassessment notice issued to give effect to a finding or direction in an appellate, revisional, or reference order under the repealed income-tax law, subject to the statutory restriction on reopening based on such a finding or direction.
material_facts: The original individual assessments for the relevant years were completed under the repealed income-tax law without including income from former joint-family properties.

In proceedings concerning the family’s assessments, appellate and reference decisions under the repealed law accepted a partial partition, making income from some properties assessable to the individual.
No proceedings concerning that income were pending under the repealed law when the new law came into force.

The tax authority later issued reassessment notices under the new law through the transitional provision, seeking to give effect to those decisions, although the ordinary reassessment time limit had expired.
issues.conclusion: The notices were not barred by the ordinary time limit. The transitional provision must be read to allow the reassessment provisions, including the enlargement of time under section 150(1), to apply with the necessary modifications, subject to section 150(2). The appeal was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 297(2)(d)(ii) and 150(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, the transitional reassessment provision is read mutatis mutandis so that section 150(1) can lift the ordinary time bar where reassessment is initiated to give effect to a finding or direction in an order made under the repealed Act; the saving remains subject to section 150(2). This construction preserves continuity across repeal and avoids an anomalous gap. The Court applied the continuity approach reflected in Third Income Tax Officer v. Damodar Bhat and Jain Bros. v. Union of India. It distinguished Jain v. Mahendra and Govinddas v. Income Tax Officer, and held that Seth Gujarmal Modi v. Commissioner of Income Tax was not conclusive on this issue. It also noted that section 297(2)(k) could be read liberally to deem the relevant earlier orders to have been made under the corresponding provisions of the new Act.

rule.if: transitional_reassessment_proceeding and escaped_income_not_assessed and no_old_law_proceeding_pending and prior_order_under_repealed_law and reassessment_gives_effect_to_prior_finding and not statutory_reopening_bar

predicates.transitional_reassessment_proceeding: A reassessment is initiated under a new law’s transitional process for income relating to an earlier assessment period.
predicates.escaped_income_not_assessed: Income was left out of the taxpayer’s assessment because it was treated as assessable in another person’s or entity’s hands.
predicates.no_old_law_proceeding_pending: No proceeding concerning that income was pending under the repealed law when the new law took effect.
predicates.prior_order_under_repealed_law: An authority made an order under the repealed law that contains a finding or direction relevant to the income.
predicates.reassessment_gives_effect_to_prior_findi: The reassessment is initiated to give effect to the finding or direction in the earlier order.
predicates.statutory_reopening_bar: A statutory restriction independently prohibits reassessment based on the earlier finding or direction.

issues.definition: When a transitional reassessment concerns previously unassessed income, no earlier-law proceeding was pending, and the reassessment gives effect to a relevant earlier order, the ordinary time limit does not bar reassessment unless a separate statutory restriction prohibits it.
